why_items.title: Science-Based
why_items.desc: Synthesized from trusted medical research — not tips or fleeting trends.
details: All content is synthesized from trusted sources: WHO, PubMed, Harvard Medical School, American College of Sports Medicine.
No unsubstantiated tips or social media trends — only things verified through actual research.
The system clearly distinguishes: strongly proven evidence (RCT, meta-analysis), experimental findings, and personal opinions.
Applies Lifestyle Medicine principles: nutrition, exercise, sleep, and mindset are considered as one integrated whole.
Regularly updated with new evidence — not rigidly tied to outdated theories.

why_items.title: Simple & Practical
why_items.desc: 10 minutes a day is enough to start. Every guide is designed specifically for busy people.
details: Research shows 10–20 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise per day is enough to improve cardiovascular health, mood, and sleep quality.
Daily Core Framework: 5 min warm-up → 10–20 min main workout → 5 min cooldown → 5 min mind reset. Total 25–35 min, flexible to shorten when busy.
No gym or special equipment needed — all exercises can be done at home in as little as 2m² of space.
Habit Stacking principle: attach new habits to existing ones (brewing coffee → 5 min stretch; brushing teeth → 5 min mindfulness).
No-pressure philosophy: missing one day is fine — just continue tomorrow, no need to restart.

why_items.title: Clear Roadmap
why_items.desc: 7 days → 12 weeks → 24 weeks. Small steps, never feel overwhelmed or give up.
details: 🌱 Phase 1 — 7-Day Kickstart: Learn 3 basic habits (morning movement, adequate protein, regular sleep). Goal: don't quit after the first week.
💪 Phase 2 — Weeks 2–12: Build your foundation. Gradually add personalized nutrition, Weekly Rhythm, short mindfulness. Progress test every 4 weeks.
🚀 Phase 3 — Weeks 13–24: Full personalization. Adjust intensity to your specific goals: weight loss, muscle gain, or overall endurance improvement.
Each week has a clear checklist — know exactly where you are and what to do next. No 'gray zones'.
If you miss a day, just continue the next day — no need to restart your entire journey.

why_items.title: 360° Complete
why_items.desc: Movement · Nutrition · Lifestyle · Mind · Knowledge · Tools — no angle left behind.
details: 🏃 Movement & Exercise: Daily Core 20–40 min, Weekly Rhythm (3 strength + 2 cardio + 2 recovery days). Applied sports science.
🥗 Nutrition & Meal Plans: Personalized TDEE based on weight, height, and lifestyle. Practical 7-day meal plans — no starvation, balanced macros.
🌿 Healthy Lifestyle: Optimize sleep, morning sunlight exposure, proper hydration. Small changes, big impact.
🧘 Mindful Living: 3-step meditation for beginners, box breathing (Navy SEAL technique), evidence-based stress management.
📚 Health Knowledge: Understand your body to make smart decisions — reading food labels, understanding health indicators, recognizing warning signs.
🛠️ Tools & Resources: Daily/weekly checklists, meal templates, 4-week assessment tests — download and use immediately.

reviews.title: How They Transformed
reviews.sub: 2,400+ people living healthier every day — here are their stories

items.text: I used to think working out needed at least an hour to be effective. After 30 days with the Daily Core 20-minute framework, I lost 3kg and sleep so much better. I had no idea it could be this simple!
The TDEE calculator and 7-day meal plan are very practical. I did not have to starve at all, just adjusted my macro ratios. Gained 4kg of quality muscle in 12 weeks.
The meditation and box breathing genuinely changed how I handle stress. After 3 weeks of morning practice, I am much calmer in tense classroom situations.
I am 42 and started with the 7-day program because I was afraid I could not keep up. Now at week 10 of the 12-week journey. Energy is noticeably higher and no more afternoon slumps.
As a medical student I am picky about sources. The content here is evidence-based without over-marketing. Already recommended it to my entire study group.
I now use the 3+2+2 weekly rhythm to schedule my clients — solid structure, easy to sustain. The weekly checklist helps them self-track without me having to remind them.
Healthy recipes the whole family loves, no expensive ingredients needed. A 50% veggie plate that tastes better than restaurant food. My 8-year-old even eats more willingly now!
The material on circadian rhythm and sleep is excellent — I even reference it when advising patients. Rare to find a Vietnamese source this well-curated.

items.role: Office Worker · Ho Chi Minh City
items.text: The Weekly Rhythm training schedule is very sensible. I have followed it 8 consecutive weeks — a personal record! Only wish there were more movement tutorial videos.
The 7-day meal plan is delicious and easy to prepare, my wife loves it too. Some ingredients are a bit hard to find locally. More substitution options would make it perfect.
The content is solid and well-structured, but as a complete beginner there is a lot of information and I sometimes did not know where to start. Hope to see a simpler quick-start guide.
The meditation theory is good but hard to apply in a busy life. The 5-minute daily exercises are doable, but the longer sessions are still a challenge for me.

tips.title: Consistency over intensity
tips.desc: Training 3–5 times/week consistently beats heavy sessions followed by long breaks. 20 min daily beats 2 hours monthly.

tips.title: Progressive overload
tips.desc: Increase no more than 10% volume or sets per week. This rule prevents injury and burnout over the long term.

tips.title: Sleep is the recovery drug
tips.desc: 7–9h every night. Muscles grow while you sleep, not while you train. Sleep deprivation reduces performance by 20–30%.

tips.title: Hit your protein daily
tips.desc: 1.6–2g protein/kg bodyweight. Prioritize whole foods: eggs, lean meat, tofu, Greek yogurt.

tips.title: Keep a training journal
tips.desc: Just 5 min per session: log sets, reps, how you felt. Journals let you see progress when your body cannot.

tips.title: Be patient with results
tips.desc: Real results come after 4–8 weeks of consistent training. The early weeks are your body learning, not being lazy.

A.title: Learn 6 Fundamental Movements
A.detail: Squat · Hinge · Push · Pull · Core · Breath
A.note: Perfect form before load. Don't worry about reps — that's your only goal today.
details: These 6 movement patterns cover ~95% of functional movements in daily life and sports — mastering them is the foundation for all future progress.
Day 1 requires no high reps or heavy weight — the goal is to feel the correct muscles working. Once form is solid, reps and weight will naturally follow.
The brain needs 300–500 correct repetitions to install a motor pattern into autopilot. This is why training 3–4×/week in the first 4 weeks matters more than training a lot right away.

points.label: Squat + Hinge
points.note: Lower body — quads, glutes, lower back

points.label: Push + Pull
points.note: Upper body balance — prevents shoulder imbalance

points.label: Form before volume
points.note: Technique builds the base — reps come later

B.title: Eat 3 Protein-Rich Meals
B.detail: 2 eggs morning · chicken breast lunch · fish/tofu dinner
B.note: No need to cut carbs. Add veg and reduce sweets — enough for day one.
details: Protein is the building block for muscle, tissue repair, and hormones — you don't need a lot, but you need it consistently at every meal to see results.
One palm of protein per meal is the simplest rule: no measuring, works when eating out, and sufficient for most people at a maintenance level.
No need to 'eat clean' 100% on day one. Simply adding protein to your existing meals is enough to create meaningful change.

points.label: Dinner: fish/tofu
points.note: Easy to digest, light for the evening

points.label: Water + absorption
points.note: Drink enough water to help the body process protein

C.title: Sleep Before 11 PM
C.detail: Dark + cool room · phone away from bed · 7–9h
C.note: More important than any workout — priority #1.
details: Cortisol naturally drops after 10:30 PM — sleeping before 11 PM aligns with your circadian rhythm, leading to deeper sleep, easier waking, and better recovery.
Blue light from phones suppresses melatonin by up to 50% — keep your phone out of the bedroom or enable night mode at least 1 hour before bed.
A cool room (64–72°F / 18–22°C) and complete darkness are the two most important physical factors that determine sleep depth.

points.label: Target 11 PM
points.note: Bedtime, not just time to lie down

points.label: Phone away from bed
points.note: Keep it out of the room or face-down

points.label: 64–72°F / 18–22°C
points.note: Optimal room temperature for deep sleep

D.title: 3 Deep Breaths on Waking
D.note: 30 seconds sets an anchor for the whole day.
details: In the morning, cortisol rises rapidly (Cortisol Awakening Response) — 3 slow deep breaths activate the parasympathetic system, reducing reflexive stress right at the start of the day.
4s inhale – 4s hold – 4s exhale is the simplest form of box breathing. Navy SEALs use this technique to stay calm under extreme pressure.
Just 30 seconds creates a positive 'anchor': the brain links waking up with calm instead of stress. After 21 days, this habit becomes automatic.

points.label: 3 cycles
points.note: 30 seconds is enough to shift the brain's mode

A.title: Repeat 6 Movements + Add 1 Set
A.detail: Same workout · add 1 set per movement
A.note: The brain learns through repetition — don't skip it even if it feels too simple.
details: The brain learns through correct repetition — not through variety. Day 2 with the same 6 exercises is far better motor learning than switching to new ones.
The simplest progressive overload: +1 set per exercise. Yesterday 2 sets → today 3 sets. Gradual adaptation is more sustainable than shocking the body.
Log each session: reps, perceived effort (1–10), form notes. This small data will transform how you train.

points.label: Log your session
points.note: Reps + effort level after each workout

B.title: Protein at Every Main Meal
B.note: 1 palm of protein per meal — the simplest rule to avoid protein shortfall.
details: The amino acid pool in the blood needs replenishing every 4–5 hours — eating protein evenly across 3 meals is more effective than eating a large amount once.
Muscle Protein Synthesis (MPS) — the muscle-building process — only activates when sufficient leucine is present. It's found in animal protein and legumes. Aim for 20–30g per meal.
You don't need to eat pure meat — combining plant protein (tofu, lentils, oats) with animal protein gives you a complete amino acid profile.

points.label: ~120g total/day
points.note: For a 60kg person with moderate activity

C.title: 10-Minute Morning Routine
C.detail: Drink water · 5 min sunlight · write 1 daily goal
C.note: A morning anchor helps the brain switch on earlier.
details: Cortisol naturally peaks in the first 30–45 minutes after waking — this is when the brain is most active. Capitalize on this with a morning routine instead of scrolling.
Natural morning light resets the circadian clock and activates serotonin — even 5 minutes standing by a window or balcony is enough.
Write 1 daily intention in under one line: the brain will automatically seek opportunities to fulfill it throughout the day, thanks to the reticular activating system.

points.label: 5 min sunlight
points.note: A window or balcony is enough

D.title: 3-Line Evening Journal
D.detail: What went well · what I learned · what to do tomorrow
D.note: 5 min before bed. Doesn't need to be good — just honest.
details: Writing down something positive from the day activates dopamine and serotonin — the brain 'learns' that today had value, reducing pre-sleep anxiety.
3 simple questions: What went well? What did I learn? What will I do tomorrow? No need for length or perfection — just be honest.
Handwriting beats typing: pen and paper engage deeper brain processing, helping memories consolidate better during sleep.

A.title: Brisk Walk 20 Minutes
A.detail: Light cardio · heart rate 100–120 · muscle recovery
A.note: Walk after lunch: lowers blood sugar 20–30%, builds base endurance.
details: A brisk walk after lunch reduces post-meal blood sugar spikes by 20–30%, improving insulin sensitivity and reducing the afternoon energy slump.
Low-intensity cardio (heart rate 100–120 bpm) actually helps muscle recovery better than sitting still — it increases blood flow to muscles without adding fatigue.
20 minutes of walking accumulates 2,000–2,500 steps — covering 25–30% of the daily 8,000-step goal, with no equipment needed.

B.title: Handle Eating Out Smartly
B.detail: 1 protein + 2 veg + moderate carbs = the eating-out formula
B.note: No need to avoid social meals — just use a simple strategy.
details: Formula 1P+2V+S: 1 portion protein + 2 portions vegetables + moderate starch. Works at any restaurant — no need to read nutrition labels.
Choose your protein first, then pick sides — this order reduces the chance of ending up with a meal that's too low in protein.
Don't skip social meals — that creates more psychological cost than eating an extra 100 kcal. Smart eating out is 100× more sustainable than strict clean eating.

points.label: Protein first
points.note: Choose your main protein source first

points.label: Moderate starch
points.note: ½ bowl rice/noodles — no need to eliminate

C.title: No Phone 30 Min Before Bed
C.detail: Replace with: reading · breathing · light stretching
C.note: Blue light suppresses melatonin — one small habit improves sleep depth.
details: Blue light (480nm) from screens suppresses melatonin by up to 50%. It takes 30–60 minutes for hormone levels to recover after turning off the screen.
Scrolling social media at night triggers a dopamine loop — the brain can't switch off even when your eyes are tired. This is why you feel 'not sleepy' after lying down for a while.
Replace the last 30 minutes with reading a physical book or light stretching — both naturally lower heart rate and prepare the body for sleep.

points.label: Dopamine loop
points.note: Brain can't switch off even when eyes are tired

points.label: Replace with a book
points.note: Physical books don't emit blue light

points.label: Or light stretching
points.note: 5–10 min stretch = sleep signal for the brain

D.title: Box Breathing 5 Minutes
D.detail: Inhale 4 · hold 4 · exhale 4 · hold 4 — repeat 5 rounds
D.note: Use when stressed, before meetings, or before bed.
details: Box breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system (rest-and-digest) — the opposite of the sympathetic system (fight-or-flight). Just 4–5 cycles produce a noticeable shift.
Navy SEALs use this 4-4-4-4 technique to stay calm under extreme pressure — its effectiveness is backed by multiple neuroscience studies.
5 minutes = 5 cycles, enough to reduce heart rate by 10–15 bpm and significantly lower cortisol. Use it before a stressful meeting or at night before sleep.

points.label: Inhale 4s
points.note: Breathe from the belly, slow and steady

A.title: Active Recovery 15 Minutes
A.detail: Stretch · foam roll · light yoga · no heavy training
A.note: Recovery = invisible training. Muscles grow at rest, not during effort.
details: Muscles grow while resting, not while training — heavy exercise only creates the stimulus. Recovery is when the body actually builds strength.
Foam rolling breaks up adhesions in muscle tissue and increases blood flow to the muscle — reducing DOMS (post-workout soreness) more effectively than complete rest.
Light yoga (restorative yoga) combined with deep breathing activates the parasympathetic system — reducing cortisol and improving sleep quality that night.

B.title: Vegetable Priority Day
B.detail: Salad · soup · steamed veg · more than usual
B.note: Fiber feeds gut bacteria — immune system and mood both benefit.
details: 70% of the immune system resides in the gut — gut bacteria need fiber (prebiotics) from leafy greens to function well, produce serotonin, and reduce inflammation.
A variety of colorful vegetables means a variety of phytochemicals and vitamins: dark green (folate, iron), red/orange (lycopene, beta-carotene), purple (anthocyanins).
1,300 kcal on a veggie-light day doesn't mean hunger — fiber keeps you full longer than starch because it doesn't digest quickly. Full belly, lower calories.

C.title: 8,000 Steps + Sunlight
C.detail: Total 8k steps through the day · 5 min morning sunlight
C.note: No need to walk continuously. Steps accumulate throughout the day.
details: 8,000 steps per day don't have to be continuous — research shows that total steps accumulated throughout the day (walking around the house, taking stairs, going outside) have the same benefit.
5 minutes of morning sunlight (6–9 AM) resets the circadian clock and triggers vitamin D production — both directly impact energy levels and mood.
A step-counting app (built into your phone) helps you realize how much you've actually walked — usually less than you think, and more once you start paying attention.

points.label: Step-counting app
points.note: Already built into your phone's health app

D.title: Meditation 5 Minutes
D.detail: Sit · close eyes · focus on breath · no judgment
D.note: You don't need to empty your mind — just notice and gently return to breath.
details: Meditation doesn't require 'no thoughts' — that's the most common misconception. The goal is simply to notice when the mind wanders and gently return to the breath.
The Default Mode Network (active when 'doing nothing') is linked to anxiety and overthinking. Meditation reduces DMN activity — reducing worry about the future and past.
5 minutes of daily meditation is enough to see results after 8 weeks: lower cortisol, increased gray matter in the prefrontal cortex, improved emotional regulation.

points.label: Sit comfortably
points.note: Chair, floor, or bed — all fine

points.label: Focus on the breath
points.note: Feel the belly rise and fall

points.label: No judgment
points.note: Thoughts arise = notice them, return to breath

A.title: Full-Body Strength 30 Minutes
A.detail: 3 sets/exercise · Squat + Lunge + Push + Row + Plank
A.note: RPE 7/10 — feel tired but not depleted. That is the right zone.
details: RPE 7/10 is the right zone — feel tired, could do 3 more reps if needed, but not exhausted. This zone triggers adaptation without causing overtraining.
Compound movements (Squat, Lunge, Push, Row, Plank) activate multiple muscle groups simultaneously — more efficient than isolation exercises in the same 30 minutes.
Progressive overload on day 5: if you did 10 Squats × 2 sets on day 1, today do 12 reps × 3 sets. Small steady increases beat large sporadic ones.

points.label: RPE 7/10
points.note: Tired but form is still solid

points.label: Progressive overload
points.note: +1–2 reps or +1 set vs last week

B.title: Carbs Before + Protein After Training
B.detail: Before: banana · After: rice + chicken · ~1,620 kcal
B.note: Carbs = fuel. Protein = muscle-building material. Don't skip the post-workout meal.
details: Eat carbs 30–60 minutes before training: glycogen (muscle fuel) needs to be topped up. A banana or bread is a quick, easy-to-digest option that won't weigh you down.
The anabolic window post-workout (30–90 min): the body absorbs protein and carbs most efficiently to repair and build muscle. Skipping this meal wastes your workout.
1,620 kcal on a training day is more than the usual 1,410 kcal — the body needs extra energy for muscle building and recovery. This isn't overeating, it's eating right.

points.label: Carbs = fuel
points.note: Glycogen lets muscles perform at max

points.label: Protein = material
points.note: Amino acids build muscle during sleep

C.title: Optimize Tonight's Sleep
C.detail: 18–22C · complete darkness · no caffeine after 2 PM
C.note: Sleep after heavy training = the most critical time for muscle repair.
details: Growth hormone (GH) is released mainly during deep sleep from 11 PM–1 AM — this is when muscles truly regenerate after a hard workout. Missing sleep wastes your training effort.
Caffeine has a half-life of 5–7 hours — a coffee at 3 PM still has 50% caffeine in the bloodstream at 10 PM, significantly reducing deep sleep quality.
A completely dark room matters more than most people realize — light through closed eyelids still suppresses melatonin. Blackout curtains or a sleep mask solve this.

points.label: 64–72°F / 18–22°C
points.note: Cooler temperature signals sleep to the brain

points.label: GH peaks 11 PM–1 AM
points.note: Sleeping on time maximizes training gains

D.title: Set Morning Intention
D.detail: Write 1 sentence: Today I will ___ then read it aloud
D.note: Clear intention leads to ~35% more consistent action.
details: An intention differs from a goal — an intention is a specific action for today, not a long-term outcome. 'I will train at 6 AM today' is far clearer than 'I want to be healthy'.
Writing it down and reading it aloud activates the Reticular Activating System (RAS) — the brain's filter will notice opportunities to fulfill the intention throughout the day.
Research by Peter Gollwitzer (NYU) on implementation intentions shows that writing 'I will do X at Y in Z' increases follow-through from 39% to 91%.

points.label: Write 1 specific sentence
points.note: 'At 6 AM I will train in the living room'

points.label: Review tonight
points.note: Did I do it? What did I learn today?

A.title: Light Yoga / Walk 30 Minutes
A.detail: Active recovery · no heavy training on first weekend
A.note: Weekend = recharge time. Don't let training pressure damage your motivation.
details: The first weekend should be about recharging, not exhaustion. The pressure to train hard every day is the top reason beginners quit.
Light yoga (yin or restorative yoga) increases parasympathetic tone — helping the body and mind shift from 'survive mode' to 'recover mode'.
A 30-minute outdoor walk boosts endorphins, vitamin D, and serotonin — 3 mental health benefits that require no gym or equipment.

points.label: Yoga 20–30 min
points.note: Yin or restorative yoga is ideal

B.title: Meal Prep 45 Minutes
B.detail: Cook 2 proteins · veg · carbs · portion into containers
B.note: Meal prep eliminates 60% of impulsive food decisions — set the environment to win.
details: Decision fatigue (exhaustion from making choices) is the real cause of unhealthy eating — not lack of willpower. Meal prep eliminates those decisions.
45 minutes on the weekend saves ~2 hours during the week — no more wondering 'what do I eat today', no ordering fast food because nothing is ready, no skipping meals when busy.
Basic batch cooking: cook 2 proteins (chicken + eggs), 1 large batch of vegetables, 1 pot of rice/potatoes. Divide into containers = 4–5 lunches ready.

points.label: 45 min = saves 2 hrs
points.note: No need to cook 4–5 weekday lunches

points.label: 2 proteins ready
points.note: Boiled chicken + boiled eggs = most flexible

points.label: Pre-cut vegetables
points.note: Salads and stir-fries are faster this way

points.label: Pre-portioned containers
points.note: Open and eat — removes decisions = success

C.title: Tidy Your Space
C.detail: Desk clean · bedroom tidy · fridge organized
C.note: Tidy space reduces cortisol 20% — directly impacts sleep quality and focus.
details: A cluttered space continuously activates the brain's threat-processing area — creating a low-level 'background stress' even when you're not aware of it. Tidying up genuinely reduces cortisol.
Arrange the fridge with a 'healthy default' — vegetables and protein at eye level, snacks at the back. Your environment determines 80% of your eating behavior.
A tidy bedroom = the brain knows this is a rest space. When a work desk and belongings are in the bedroom, the brain can't fully switch off.

points.label: Clear the work desk
points.note: Only keep what you need for today

points.label: Bedroom = rest space
points.note: No work desk in the bedroom

D.title: 10-Minute Weekly Review
D.detail: What went well · what needs work · what to improve next week
D.note: Weekly review = the fastest growth tool. Turn experiences into lessons.
details: A weekly review is the growth tool used by most high-performers and CEOs — it turns 7 days of experience into actionable lessons for the next week.
3 core questions: (1) What did I do well this week? (2) What needs improvement? (3) What will I improve by just 1 thing next week? Only 1 — no need to change everything at once.
Don't be overly self-critical — a weekly review is a learning tool, not a courtroom. The goal is to reflect with curiosity, not guilt.

points.label: What went well
points.note: Acknowledge it, even if small — builds momentum

points.label: Plan the coming week
points.note: Schedule workouts + meal plan in advance

A.title: Complete Rest Day
A.detail: Rest day · gentle walk if you like · focus on recovery
A.note: Rest day is not failure. Your body is building strength from last week's training.
details: Supercompensation — the body doesn't just recover to its baseline but builds further to prepare for a similar load. Rest day = an investment, not a waste.
Rest day doesn't mean lying still — a light 20–30 minute walk increases blood flow, reduces DOMS, and helps muscles recover faster than complete inactivity.
Feeling like you 'have to train to feel okay' on a rest day is a sign of attachment, not lack of recovery. Notice this feeling and let it pass — this is also mindset training.

points.label: Sleep a bit more
points.note: Rest day = permission for extra 30 min

B.title: Light, Easy-to-Digest Meals
B.note: Let your digestive system rest — less processed, more produce, enough water.
details: The digestive system also needs rest — eating light, easy-to-digest meals one day a week reduces gut inflammation and improves nutrient absorption for the next week.
Congee, soup, and vegetable broth are the easiest to digest: low in rough fiber, high in water, low energy cost to process. The digestive system gets a well-deserved break.
1,240 kcal is lower than usual because you're not training hard today — energy demand is lower, no need to force yourself to eat more. Listen to your body.

points.label: Vegetable soup/broth
points.note: Easy to digest, high water content, low calorie

points.label: Congee/porridge
points.note: Lightest on the gut — least enzyme needed

points.label: Drink more water
points.note: 2–2.5L on rest day to flush toxins

C.title: Plan the New Week
C.detail: Schedule training · prep meal plan · review goals
C.note: Preparation = winning 80% — no daily improvisation needed.
details: Planning removes friction — when you've already set 'Monday 6:30 AM workout', the brain doesn't need to decide again. Every small decision drains willpower — planning saves it for what matters.
A grocery list prepared on Sunday means no missing healthy ingredients mid-week. A fridge full of healthy food = no need to order fast food because 'there's nothing to eat'.
Reviewing your 3-month goals every Sunday helps check whether this week's actions are on the right track. Adjusting early is better than adjusting after going the wrong way for too long.

D.title: 7-Day Wrap-Up
D.detail: 3 wins · 1 area to improve · 1 commitment going forward
D.note: Look back to learn and move forward with more insight — not to criticize yourself.
details: Completing 7 days is a bigger milestone than you think — most people who try a new habit quit before day 4. This is proof you're different from the majority.
3 things done (even small) + 1 to improve + 1 commitment going forward: this structure balances acknowledgment with learning — not too self-critical, not too complacent.
Share your 7-day results with one person — an accountability partner increases continuation rates by up to 65%, according to the American Society of Training & Development.

faqs.q: Who is the Health & Lifestyle website for?
faqs.a: The website is for anyone who wants to improve their health — from complete beginners to those with a foundation looking to systematize their routine. No experience, no special equipment, no strict diet required. Just 20 minutes a day and consistency.

faqs.q: Is all content on the website completely free?
faqs.a: Yes — 100% free. All 6 pillars, 7-day / 12-week / 24-week programs, exercise videos, checklists, tracking tools and resources are completely free. Our goal is to make science-based health knowledge accessible to everyone without financial barriers.

faqs.q: Where should I start if I'm a complete beginner?
faqs.a: Start on the "Journey" page → choose "7-Day Kickstart". The first seven days are designed to gradually introduce all 4 core pillars (movement · nutrition · lifestyle · mind) without overwhelming you. Each day only requires 20–30 minutes.

faqs.q: Is the content evidence-based?
faqs.a: Yes. All content is built on modern medical research and guidelines from reputable organizations (WHO, ACSM, AHA). However, this website is educational — it does not replace personal medical advice. If you have specific health concerns, consult a doctor.

faqs.q: What does the 360° Health system include?
faqs.a: 6 pillars form a comprehensive health system: (A) Movement & Exercise — strong body; (B) Nutrition & Meal Planning — right fuel; (C) Healthy Lifestyle — sleep, steps, recovery; (D) Calm Mind — emotional balance; (E) Health Knowledge — understand your body; (F) Tools & Resources — track and maintain.

faqs.q: How many times a week should I exercise?
faqs.a: For beginners, 3 sessions/week (every other day) is ideal. Recommended structure: 3 strength sessions · 2 light cardio · 2 active recovery days. More important than frequency is consistency — 3 regular sessions over 12 weeks beats 5 sessions/week for 2 weeks then quitting.

faqs.q: What are the 6 fundamental movements and why are they important?
faqs.a: 6 foundational movement patterns: Squat (knee bend), Hinge (hip fold), Push (press), Pull (row), Core (stability) and Breathe. These are the 6 movement groups the human body performs daily. Mastering these with proper form before adding load is rule #1 to prevent injury and build a sustainable foundation.

faqs.q: Can I follow the program without any equipment?
faqs.a: Absolutely. The entire Phase 1 program (7 days + first 4 weeks) uses 100% bodyweight — no equipment needed. From week 5 you can add dumbbells or resistance bands for extra challenge, but they are not required.

faqs.q: I have chronic back pain — can I still follow the program?
faqs.a: It depends on the cause and severity. The program includes "Active Recovery" and "Stretching" sections suitable for mild back pain. However, if back pain is caused by a spinal condition or is under medical treatment, consult a doctor or physiotherapist first. Golden rule: acute pain = rest; mild chronic pain = gentle controlled movement.

faqs.q: Do I have to count calories?
faqs.a: Not required, especially in the early stages. The "Plate Model" (½ vegetables · ¼ protein · ¼ carbs) and the "1 palm of protein per meal" rule help you eat right without counting. Calorie counting is only useful at an advanced stage when you want more precise optimization.

faqs.q: What is TDEE and do I need to calculate it?
faqs.a: TDEE (Total Daily Energy Expenditure) is the total calories your body burns each day. Knowing your TDEE helps you eat the right amount for your goal: weight loss (TDEE − 400 kcal), maintenance (= TDEE), muscle gain (TDEE + 300 kcal). The TDEE calculator is in the B0 Toolkit on the Nutrition page.

faqs.q: I eat out a lot for work — can I still follow the nutrition guidelines?
faqs.a: Yes. The smart eating-out formula: "1 protein + 2 vegetables + moderate carbs". At restaurants: order extra vegetables or salad, choose grilled/steamed protein instead of fried, control carb portions. No need to refuse social meals — just apply a simple strategy.

faqs.q: Do I need to use supplements?
faqs.a: Not in the early stages. Whole foods are always the foundation — supplements only work when nutrition is already solid. If considering: Vitamin D3 (if rarely outdoors), Omega-3 (if low fish intake), Protein Whey (if struggling to get enough protein from food). Consult a doctor before taking any supplements.

faqs.q: How much water should I drink daily?
faqs.a: Simple formula: body weight (kg) × 35ml. Example: 60kg → 2.1 liters/day. Sign of adequate hydration: pale yellow urine. Add 500ml when exercising. Drink evenly throughout the day and start with a large glass of water immediately on waking.

faqs.q: How many hours of sleep do I need?
faqs.a: 7–9 hours is the recommendation for adults (WHO). More important than quantity is sleep quality and regularity — sleeping and waking at the same time every day (including weekends) matters more than sleeping extra on weekends to catch up.

faqs.q: What is NEAT and why is it more important than I think?
faqs.a: NEAT (Non-Exercise Activity Thermogenesis) is the energy burned from all activities outside formal exercise — walking, standing, climbing stairs, doing chores. NEAT can account for 15–50% of total daily calories burned. Goal: 8,000–10,000 steps/day.

faqs.q: What does a minimal morning routine require?
faqs.a: A 10-minute morning routine is enough to make a difference: (1) Drink a large glass of water; (2) Get 5 minutes of natural sunlight; (3) Write 1 goal for the day. No need to wake up at 5 AM — just do it consistently.

faqs.q: How can I improve sleep quality fastest?
faqs.a: Three most effective interventions: (1) No screens 30 minutes before bed; (2) Keep bedroom at 18–22°C and completely dark; (3) No caffeine after 2 PM. Apply all three correctly for 7 days — you will notice a clear difference.

faqs.q: I've never meditated before — how do I start?
faqs.a: The simplest meditation: sit comfortably, close your eyes, focus on your breath for 5 minutes. When your mind wanders, gently bring attention back to your breath — without judgment. Start with 5 minutes each morning, gradually increasing to 10–15 minutes after 2 weeks.

faqs.q: What is Box Breathing and when should I use it?
faqs.a: Box Breathing: Inhale 4s → Hold 4s → Exhale 4s → Hold 4s → repeat. This technique activates the parasympathetic nervous system, reducing cortisol and heart rate within 2–3 minutes. Use when: stressed before a meeting, struggling to sleep, or before a workout.

faqs.q: I have no time to meditate — is there a way?
faqs.a: "Micro-meditation" works for busy lives: (1) 3 conscious deep breaths each morning (30 seconds); (2) Eat mindfully — no phone; (3) 5-minute mindful walk midday. These small moments add up to build a solid mental foundation.

faqs.q: What should I write in a health journal?
faqs.a: The 3-line evening journal formula (3–5 minutes): (1) "Today I did well..." — note 1 positive thing; (2) "I learned..." — 1 lesson or observation; (3) "Tomorrow I will..." — 1 specific action. After 4 weeks, looking back you will see your own patterns much more clearly.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the 7-day, 12-week, and 24-week programs?
faqs.a: 7-Day Kickstart: Introduce all 4 pillars, form baseline habits. 12-Week Foundation: 3 phases building foundation → increasing load → personalizing. 24-Week Advanced: Expand to all 6 full pillars, including medical knowledge and carb cycling.

faqs.q: How much time do I need per day?
faqs.a: Daily Core structure 20–40 min: 5 min warm-up · 10–20 min main workout · 5–10 min cool-down · 5 min mind reset. Plus: 10-min morning routine + 5-min evening journal. Total: 35–55 min/day. No day requires more than 1 hour.

faqs.q: Can I skip the 7 days and go straight to the 12-week program?
faqs.a: You can, but it is not recommended. The first 7 days help you understand how your body responds to change, identify weaknesses, and build psychological momentum. People who skip the 7 days tend to quit earlier. If you already have a solid base (consistent training for 6+ months), you can start from Phase 2 of the 12-week program.

faqs.q: What should I do if I miss 1–2 days in the program?
faqs.a: No worries. The rule: "Never miss twice in a row". Miss 1 day → continue from the next day, no need to make up. Miss 1 week → restart from the beginning of that week. 80% consistency over 12 weeks beats 100% for 3 weeks then quitting.

faqs.q: What is the BMR (Basal Metabolic Rate) formula?
faqs.a: BMR uses the Mifflin-St Jeor formula: Male = (10 × weight kg) + (6.25 × height cm) − (5 × age) + 5. Female = (10 × weight kg) + (6.25 × height cm) − (5 × age) − 161. Example: Male 30 years, 70kg, 170cm → BMR = 700 + 1062.5 − 150 + 5 = 1617.5 kcal/day. This is the minimum energy your body needs at complete rest.

faqs.q: How is TDEE calculated? What are the activity multipliers?
faqs.a: TDEE = BMR × Activity Multiplier. Levels: Sedentary (desk job, no exercise) × 1.2; Light (1–3 sessions/week) × 1.375; Moderate (3–5 sessions/week) × 1.55; Active (6–7 sessions/week) × 1.725; Very Active (2× daily training) × 1.9. Example: BMR 1617 kcal × 1.55 (moderate) = 2506 kcal TDEE.

faqs.q: How many calories should I eat based on my goal?
faqs.a: Adjust from your TDEE: Weight loss = TDEE − 400 kcal (moderate deficit, not extreme); Maintenance = TDEE; Muscle gain = TDEE + 300 kcal (small surplus). Never eat below your BMR. Example with TDEE 2500: weight loss = 2100 kcal, muscle gain = 2800 kcal.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my macro ratios (protein, fat, carbs)?
faqs.a: Step 1 — Protein: body weight × 1.6–2.0g (use 2.0g for weight loss or muscle gain; 1.6g for maintenance). Step 2 — Fat: 25% of total calories ÷ 9 (since 1g fat = 9 kcal). Step 3 — Carbs fill the rest: (Total kcal − Protein×4 − Fat×9) ÷ 4. Example: 70kg, 2100 kcal weight loss — Protein 140g (560 kcal) · Fat 58g (525 kcal) · Carbs 254g (1016 kcal).

faqs.q: What is the caloric density of each macronutrient?
faqs.a: Key constants: Protein = 4 kcal/g; Carbohydrates = 4 kcal/g; Fat = 9 kcal/g; Alcohol = 7 kcal/g (nearly as dense as fat, often overlooked). Practical examples: 100g chicken breast (30g protein) ≈ 120 kcal; 100g cooked rice (28g carbs) ≈ 130 kcal; 1 tablespoon cooking oil (14g fat) ≈ 126 kcal.

faqs.q: How much water do I need? What is the water intake formula?
faqs.a: Basic formula: body weight (kg) × 35ml = minimum daily water intake. Examples: 60kg × 35 = 2,100ml (2.1 liters); 75kg × 35 = 2,625ml (2.6 liters). Add: +500ml per workout session; +300ml in hot weather. Signs of adequate hydration: pale yellow urine. Signs of dehydration: dark yellow urine, dry mouth, fatigue.

faqs.q: How is BMI calculated and what do the ranges mean?
faqs.a: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ [height (m)]². Example: 68kg, 1.70m → BMI = 68 ÷ (1.70)² = 23.5. WHO classifications: Under 18.5 = Underweight; 18.5–24.9 = Normal; 25.0–29.9 = Overweight; 30.0+ = Obese. Note: BMI does not distinguish muscle from fat — muscular people may be classified as "overweight" despite excellent health. Combine with waist circumference (<90cm men, <80cm women) for more accurate assessment.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my training heart rate zones?
faqs.a: Maximum Heart Rate (HRmax) = 220 − age. Example: age 30 → HRmax = 190 bpm. Heart rate zones: 50–60% HRmax = Light warm-up (minimal aerobic benefit); 60–70% HRmax = Optimal fat-burning zone; 70–85% HRmax = Cardio zone — improves cardiovascular fitness; 85–95% HRmax = Advanced zone — for experienced athletes only. For beginners: aim for 60–75% HRmax for 20–30 minutes.
